North Korea, officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), is the communist state in the northern half of the Korean Peninsula, founded in 1948 with Pyongyang as its capital. The chart's bar is North and South Korea.

When Japan surrendered in 1945, Soviet troops took Korea north of the 38th parallel. They backed Kim Il Sung, a former guerrilla, who became leader of the new state. In 1950 he invaded the South, starting the Korean War. It ended in 1953 in a ceasefire near the old line, with no peace treaty.

Kim built a one-party state around himself and the idea of Juche, self-reliance. Power has passed down his family: to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and his grandson Kim Jong Un in 2011. After Soviet aid ended, a famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands of people. The country tested its first nuclear weapon in 2006. It remains one of the most closed societies on earth, facing a far richer South Korea.
